title: How confidence scores can increase learning
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton argues that asking students to attach a 0-10 confidence score to answers before they are marked is a cheap, high-yield practice. He grounds it in the Hypercorrection Effect, the finding that confidently held errors are the most likely to be corrected, and in his own 2021 co-authored research on confidence scores and achievement. He gives six reasons: it strengthens hypercorrection, improves metacognitive accuracy, creates investment in answers, prioritises which corrections to make first, gives the teacher better information on whom to call on, and reduces silly mistakes. He then lists where to use scores, how to choose a scale, and practical tips such as banning a 5. The move is from a research finding to concrete classroom routines with worked student examples.
points: Explicit confidence scores make students notice how sure they were, so the surprise needed for the Hypercorrection Effect is not lost by the time answers are revealed.
Scores let students prioritise corrections, starting with the errors they were most confident about, since those yield the largest learning gains.
On mini-whiteboards, a confidence score helps the teacher choose whom to question and in what order, from no response through high-confidence error to confident correct answers.
Asking for scores at the end of the work, before answers are revealed, prompts a review that catches silly mistakes better than a bare instruction to check your work.
Banning a score of 5 and experimenting with points won or lost by confidence level counter students playing it safe.
quotes: The Hypercorrection Effect is the finding that errors endorsed with higher confidence are more likely to be corrected on a final test than those with lower confidence.

Most students I have taught or observed simply complete a question and then move on to the next. If a student only finds out that they are wrong later in the lesson when the teacher goes through the answers, they may not remember how they felt about that particular question and hence not experience the surprise needed to kick-start the Hypercorrection Effect.
Once you have committed to saying you feel confident about an answer, you have skin in the game. Suddenly, that answer means something to you, and you are eager to find out whether you are right.

But that is an inefficient use of this limited amount of time. The Hypercorrection Effect tells us that errors made with high confidence will likely lead to the most significant learning gains when corrected.
Calling upon this student next may prove a magical moment as they realise that, despite their doubts, they are correct and are probably better at maths than they think.
I find this infinitely more effective than saving to students: Now go back and check your work - I know of no other string of 7 words that students ignore more.
Ban a score of 5. If you use a 0 - 10 scale, you will find lots of students play it safe and stick down a 5. Banning scores of 5 forces students to say whether they are more or less confident
